text: Nine a.m. Thursday. The general contractor called Dokgo Chul down in the Guro foundation pit. He was already counting minutes.
Seven hours to handover. Dokgo bowed to the phone and promised they were on schedule. The smile vanished when he hung up.
He passed the deadline down to the eight porters below him.
Ryu Survey set up beside the C-grade gate. Taeo regretted reading up on that grade the night before.
Nib's compulsory hard hat perched on his ears, so Haein drilled two holes in it. Nib approved. He still refused boots.
Haein's new cable could carry radio signals through the gate, as long as it stayed intact. Taeo would log Nib's calls. From outside, Minho reminded him. Again.
Dokgo wanted the scout in at ten sharp. Minho said Nib would go in when the frame was checked. Dokgo answered with the contract.
His subcontract carried a penalty of five million won an hour for late handover. And Dokgo passed the pain down to his workers.
Taeo did the maths: eighty-three thousand, three hundred and thirty-three won, every minute.
Gu Dami caught Taeo recognising her from the news. The cameras had filmed the hunters, she said. Only her back.
She knew Dokgo's story about the missing porter. She still needed the work. Bluebird wanted an instalment tomorrow, and she owed two million, one hundred thousand won.
She had borrowed for summon draws at eighteen and got two commons, leased to a warehouse for thirty thousand a month each. The interest had pulled better than she had.
Nib was studying her vest with deep admiration. Fourteen pockets. Sixteen, Dami corrected. Two more inside.
Nib made sixty thousand a day. Dami made ninety thousand, with no insurance. Taeo made nothing and stayed outside. Lucky, Dami called that.
The word landed hard. One minute of Dokgo's penalty was almost a whole day of Dami's pay.
Dokgo announced the order: scout, then porters, then the Ironclad Seven at three. 'The cheap ones go first.' Dami and Nib exchanged a look.
Dami's partner was fifty-eight-year-old Kwak Mansu. He called Nib son and recommended knee pads for the low galleries. 'I'm short,' Nib said.
Kwak's laugh turned into a wheezing cough. Dami demanded his inhaler. It was in his jacket, he said. It was fine.
Quietly, he asked her not to mention the asthma near Dokgo. Dokgo didn't pick wheezers.
Taeo watched him hang up the jacket, the blue inhaler cap poking out of the pocket. Grandpa said it was fine too.
At ten, the contractor called again. Six hours left. Minho pointed at Taeo, then at his chair.
Nib went in first, radio beside the cable. A white return mark formed on his wrist.
Taeo lurched sideways and grabbed the table. The ground had tilted. Except it hadn't, Haein said. He had felt Nib's.
The ground inside sloped left, Nib confirmed. Three seconds, then Taeo lost him again.
Was he bleeding? Haein checked. 'Not yet.'
Beyond Nib stretched a quarry of slanted stone terraces and dark galleries under a green dusk sky. Even the horizon leaned left.
The crew and the porters crossed with their loads. Dami wore number seven. Kwak wore eight.
Outside, Taeo rested his hand on the steel frame, knuckles curled for the old signal. He didn't knock.
Eleven o'clock. Five hours. Dokgo bowed to his phone again and again.
At noon, the forward camp was twenty minutes behind. The contractor put the penalty at 1,666,666 won. Dokgo promised to fix it.
He grabbed the survey handset over Haein's objection and split the porter pairs. Even numbers would take the lower gallery.
It was unsurveyed, Minho warned. Forty metres shorter, Dokgo said. And not on Ryu's survey line, so not their problem.
Taeo half rose to say something. The words didn't come.
Minho had his crew tape both ends of the lower gallery. If porters were going through it, the hazard would at least be marked.
Dami offered to take the lower route instead. Kwak told her she was faster on the upper run. He ducked under the tape and disappeared into the dark.
At one, Dokgo called roll. One through eight.
At the forward camp, number six answered. Seven, Dami, answered too. Nib was already looking toward the lower gallery's exit.
Eight didn't answer. Dokgo called Kwak Mansu by name. Kwak had never reached the forward camp, Nib reported.
Outside, Kwak's jacket still hung on its hook, the blue inhaler cap in its pocket.
He had gone into the lower gallery alone at half past twelve, Dami said. Taeo went pale.
Dokgo looked at his countdown. Less than three hours. Every minute, the same price.
Inside, Dami and Nib stared into the black gallery while the other porters shouldered their loads. Dokgo's voice came through the relay. 'He's resting somewhere. Keep moving.'
